item.text: {"chapter_id":"8B","answers":[{"question_id":"8B.1","answer":"López Obrador had a clear, multi-part program: republican austerity, anti-corruption, poverty reduction and transfers, energy and food self-sufficiency, infrastructure-led development, pacification, reduced military deployment, and cooperative foreign relations (BATCH-0024-E001; BATCH-0024-E007; BATCH-0051-E011; BATCH-0051-E012). The program was repeatedly stated in campaign materials, formal government reports, the 2022–2024 security program, and the September 2023 UN statement (BATCH-0044-E010; BATCH-0044-E011; BATCH-0048-E014). Repeated choices also revealed additional priorities: state control of strategic sectors, military-led implementation, direct transfers, and stronger executive influence over autonomous institutions (BATCH-0028-E003; BATCH-0016-E001; BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0031-E013). The program was therefore sufficiently clear to test, although it contained important tensions—especially demilitarization rhetoric versus sustained military expansion, and anti-corruption claims versus weakened transparency and oversight (BATCH-0016-E001; BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0026-E004; BATCH-0047-E009). Some stated claims were propagandistic or disputed: fact-checkers classified nine of 30 claims in the fourth-government report as true, eight as misleading, and 13 as false (BATCH-0042-E009). Attribution is strong for presidential priorities and formal initiatives, but weaker for outcomes and subordinate implementation. The evidence establishes program clarity, not program quality or success; moral worth is outside this lens.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0024-E001","BATCH-0024-E007","BATCH-0051-E011","BATCH-0051-E012","BATCH-0044-E010","BATCH-0044-E011","BATCH-0048-E014","BATCH-0028-E003","BATCH-0016-E001","BATCH-0016-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0016-E002","BATCH-0026-E004","BATCH-0047-E009","BATCH-0042-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Program statements predate 2023 and were not always consistent with later conduct.","Some stated objectives were broad, aspirational, or presented through official claims rather than independently verifiable commitments.","The evidence does not establish that every revealed priority was consciously intended as a stable program component."]},{"question_id":"8B.2","answer":"The administration translated major priorities into laws, budgets, institutions, appointments, and operating rules. Examples include the National Guard and National Public Security Program, IMSS-BIENESTAR rules, the 2023 poverty and FAIS planning framework, expanded social-program budgets, the adult pension, the medicine warehouse, and military administration of infrastructure and public functions (BATCH-0044-E010; BATCH-0044-E011; BATCH-0051-E001; BATCH-0051-E004; BATCH-0012-E001; BATCH-0049-E006; BATCH-0050-E005; BATCH-0029-E007). Security mobilization was especially concrete: military security spending rose while civil security spending and federal transfers to subnational security fell, and the National Guard expanded substantially (BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0047-E001). Positive evidence also includes formal safeguards, monitoring, certification, audit, and complaint mechanisms in the National Guard and health frameworks (BATCH-0055-E003; BATCH-0057-E003; BATCH-0051-E004; BATCH-0051-E005). However, several priorities were translated through disputed or legally defective mechanisms: the Supreme Court invalidated the transfer of National Guard control to Sedena, and Plan B electoral reforms were invalidated for procedural defects (BATCH-0055-E006; BATCH-0055-E008; BATCH-0014-E005). Appointment delays impaired INAI, IFT, and COFECE, while some analyses describe loyalty and centralization taking precedence over technical competence (BATCH-0026-E014; BATCH-0018-E015; BATCH-0026-E006). Formal authority was therefore substantial, but actual authority was constrained by Congress, courts, agencies, and subnational institutions. The record demonstrates extensive operationalization, with significant legality, capacity, and implementation qualifications.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0044-E010","BATCH-0044-E011","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0012-E001","BATCH-0049-E006","BATCH-0050-E005","BATCH-0016-E007","BATCH-0055-E003","BATCH-0051-E005"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0055-E006","BATCH-0055-E008","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0018-E015","BATCH-0026-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Many formal instruments establish design rather than executed compliance.","Congressional, judicial, subnational, and agency authority complicates personal attribution.","Some proposed reforms never became operative law."]},{"question_id":"8B.3","answer":"The administration mobilized substantial state and ruling-network resources toward selected priorities, especially the armed forces, direct transfers, flagship infrastructure, and state-owned energy firms. Military expenditure reached $11.8 billion in 2023, National Guard allocations rose to 11% of military expenditure, Guard personnel expanded, and military institutions received a dominant share of security spending (BATCH-0047-E001; BATCH-0016-E007). The government also expanded social-program funding and pension coverage, and assigned the armed forces to construction, logistics, infrastructure, medicine distribution, customs, ports, and train operations (BATCH-0052-E001; BATCH-0032-E006; BATCH-0013-E006; BATCH-0029-E007). Administrative records show real mobilization: priority programs received large budgets, CONEVAL operated extensive monitoring, and the National Guard and military training system developed personnel and organizational capacity (BATCH-0049-E006; BATCH-0054-E007; BATCH-0055-E016). The adverse side is that mobilization was uneven and often displaced civilian capacity: civil-security spending declined, health investment lagged, military secrecy limited scrutiny, and World Bank-supported objectives were frequently cancelled, restructured, or off track (BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0048-E010; BATCH-0048-E012; BATCH-0052-E015; BATCH-0052-E020). Security resources did not translate proportionately into preventive or justice activity: the Guard made a small share of prosecutor presentations, while armed confrontations rose and narcotics seizures fell (BATCH-0016-E008). Mobilization was therefore strong in volume and political direction, but selective, centralized, and inconsistently productive. Attribution to presidential priorities is strong; attribution to each expenditure, agency failure, or outcome is partial.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0047-E001","BATCH-0016-E007","BATCH-0052-E001","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0013-E006","BATCH-0049-E006","BATCH-0054-E007","BATCH-0055-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0048-E010","BATCH-0048-E012","BATCH-0052-E015","BATCH-0052-E020","BATCH-0016-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Budget and staffing data are inputs, not proof of effective use.","Many mobilization outcomes involved agencies, Congress, subnational governments, or international partners.","The evidence is strongest for security, transfers, and infrastructure, weaker for foreign policy and some social objectives."]},{"question_id":"8B.4","answer":"López Obrador appointed and empowered people and institutions capable of executing several chosen priorities, including technically experienced officials such as Banco de México governor Victoria Rodríguez Ceja and extensive military personnel for security, construction, logistics, and infrastructure operations (BATCH-0039-E001; BATCH-0055-E016; BATCH-0029-E007). Some programs also used professional evaluation, technical committees, training systems, and multidisciplinary implementation structures (BATCH-0039-E002; BATCH-0051-E004; BATCH-0055-E011). The administration replaced or reassigned officials when political or operational needs changed, including the Segalmex director and trade officials during USMCA disputes (BATCH-0046-E008; BATCH-0046-E006). Conversely, appointment backlogs left major regulators without functioning plenaries, the replacement of the National Search Commission head raised concerns about consultation and experience, and analyses describe a preference for loyalty over technical competence (BATCH-0018-E015; BATCH-0004-E008; BATCH-0026-E006). The reassignment of Ignacio Ovalle after the Segalmex scandal to another government post also suggests limited personnel discipline despite serious administrative failure (BATCH-0046-E008; BATCH-0026-E003). Military personnel were effective operators for centralized construction and coercive deployment, but their suitability for civilian policing, transparency, environmental management, and rights-protective administration was contested and often unsupported by outcomes (BATCH-0029-E007; BATCH-0031-E013; BATCH-0048-E012). Attribution is strongest for presidential appointment and empowerment choices, weaker for individual misconduct and institutional performance.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0039-E001","BATCH-0055-E016","BATCH-0029-E007","BATCH-0039-E002","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0046-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0018-E015","BATCH-0004-E008","BATCH-0026-E006","BATCH-0046-E008","BATCH-0031-E013","BATCH-0048-E012"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is no complete personnel roster or systematic performance comparison by appointment.","Qualifications and loyalty are often inferred from institutional roles rather than independently evaluated.","Some appointment and replacement decisions involved the Senate or agencies, not the president alone."]},{"question_id":"8B.5","answer":"The administration maintained substantial coordination and territorial reach in some domains. The National Public Security Program assigned monitoring and implementation duties across ministries, the health program specified federalized units and supervision, and the 2023 Otis response mobilized federal, state, military, UN, and civil-society coordination structures (BATCH-0044-E011; BATCH-0051-E002; BATCH-0051-E004; BATCH-0015-E015; BATCH-0015-E018). The Guard, military infrastructure system, social transfers, pension program, and poverty-planning instruments reached much of the country, and several programs exceeded planned coverage or output targets (BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0052-E005; BATCH-0032-E006; BATCH-0012-E003). Yet coordination frequently broke down: Ayotzinapa investigators faced military noncooperation despite presidential orders; military arrests were missing from the detention registry; health and migrant-child systems had incomplete data, staffing gaps, and inconsistent protocols; and World Bank projects were disrupted by policy changes and institutional turnover (BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0013-E003; BATCH-0009-E003; BATCH-0015-E007; BATCH-0052-E015). Major projects also experienced route changes, permit disputes, incomplete construction, and changing responsibilities (BATCH-0011-E007; BATCH-0030-E004; BATCH-0040-E008). The evidence shows strong top-down reach where the presidency and military controlled resources, but weaker horizontal coordination, civilian compliance, documentation, and milestone discipline. Presidential attribution is clear for the governing architecture and major priorities, but subordinate resistance and multi-level government limit causal certainty.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0044-E011","BATCH-0051-E002","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0015-E015","BATCH-0015-E018","BATCH-0016-E007","BATCH-0052-E005","BATCH-0032-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E002","BATCH-0013-E003","BATCH-0009-E003","BATCH-0015-E007","BATCH-0052-E015","BATCH-0011-E007","BATCH-0030-E004","BATCH-0040-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["National coverage does not establish uniform compliance or service quality.","Some coordination successes were substantially supported by UN, World Bank, or civil-society partners.","The evidence does not provide a complete milestone ledger for the whole governing portfolio."]},{"question_id":"8B.6","answer":"Many priorities became observable practice rather than remaining slogans. The government funded and expanded the older-adult pension, minimum wage, social programs, military security apparatus, IMSS-BIENESTAR, infrastructure projects, and a centralized medicine warehouse (BATCH-0032-E006; BATCH-0031-E008; BATCH-0052-E001; BATCH-0051-E001; BATCH-0013-E006). CONEVAL documented operating rules, target indicators, monitoring, and substantial evaluation activity, while UN reporting recorded labor, refugee, gender-violence, and institutional outputs (BATCH-0052-E002; BATCH-0052-E006; BATCH-0054-E007; BATCH-0015-E013; BATCH-0015-E016). Projects such as the Maya Train and Dos Bocas were physically constructed or opened, and military organizations performed assigned civilian functions (BATCH-0030-E004; BATCH-0010-E009; BATCH-0029-E007). Implementation was nonetheless partial and often poor: the Maya Train opened incomplete and over budget, health access deteriorated after institutional restructuring, medicine shortages remained severe, migrant services were overstretched, and disappearance, transparency, and security laws were not consistently enforced (BATCH-0030-E004; BATCH-0032-E003; BATCH-0013-E006; BATCH-0015-E017; BATCH-0026-E020). Audits found procurement irregularities, missing documentation, direct awards, and unresolved project expenditures (BATCH-0011-E001; BATCH-0042-E008; BATCH-0040-E008). Thus implementation was real and extensive, but uneven across sectors and often accompanied by weak controls, legal conflict, incomplete delivery, or uncertain quality. Moral evaluation is separate; the relevant issue here is conversion of chosen objectives into practice.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0031-E008","BATCH-0052-E001","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0052-E002","BATCH-0054-E007","BATCH-0015-E013","BATCH-0015-E016","BATCH-0030-E004","BATCH-0029-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0013-E006","BATCH-0015-E017","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0011-E001","BATCH-0042-E008","BATCH-0040-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Several program results are measured by administrative outputs rather than independent impact evaluations.","Some flagship-project outcomes were not mature by the end of 2023.","Subnational implementation and external partners materially affected delivery."]},{"question_id":"8B.7","answer":"Results moved toward some stated goals but not consistently across the portfolio. Poverty fell from 41.9% in 2018 to 36.3% in 2022, transfers reduced estimated poverty and extreme poverty, minimum wages rose substantially, older-person coverage expanded, and 2023 GDP growth reached 3.2% in the World Bank account (BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0032-E009; BATCH-0031-E008; BATCH-0032-E006; BATCH-0052-E014). Social spending and labor-income gains therefore provide favorable outcome evidence, although remittances, post-pandemic recovery, external demand, and other factors contributed (BATCH-0050-E003; BATCH-0032-E001; BATCH-0052-E014). Adverse outcomes were substantial: health-service deprivation rose from 16.2% to 39.1%, poverty remained high among Indigenous and disabled people, extreme poverty increased in absolute terms, GDP per capita remained below 2018 levels in some assessments, and security institutions failed to produce a clear preventive or justice gain (BATCH-0032-E003; BATCH-0032-E007; BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0016-E008). Homicides and some crimes declined from 2018, but crime rose between 2022 and 2023, impunity remained above 90%, and México Evalúa found no consistent association between greater Guard activity and homicide reduction, with possible measurement changes affecting the homicide series (BATCH-0016-E009; BATCH-0016-E010; BATCH-0016-E011). Major infrastructure outcomes were incomplete, costly, and not yet demonstrated to produce promised regional or economic benefits (BATCH-0030-E004; BATCH-0011-E006; BATCH-0029-E007). Attribution is therefore mixed: some gains plausibly reflect administration choices, but causation is confounded by inherited conditions, pandemic recovery, remittances, external markets, subnational actors, and luck.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0032-E009","BATCH-0031-E008","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0052-E014","BATCH-0050-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0032-E007","BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0016-E008","BATCH-0016-E009","BATCH-0016-E010","BATCH-0016-E011","BATCH-0030-E004","BATCH-0011-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The latest comprehensive multidimensional poverty outcomes are for 2022, released in 2023.","Many outcomes are national aggregates and cannot isolate presidential causation.","Security and macroeconomic indicators contain measurement, lag, and counterfactual uncertainty."]},{"question_id":"8B.8","answer":"There is evidence of adaptation, but it was selective and often politically or administratively incomplete. The government created commissions, revised disappearance-counting and search institutions, changed health arrangements from Seguro Popular to INSABI and then IMSS-BIENESTAR, altered infrastructure designs, expanded the medicine warehouse, and used audits, evaluations, and monitoring systems (BATCH-0004-E003; BATCH-0004-E008; BATCH-0032-E003; BATCH-0051-E001; BATCH-0011-E007; BATCH-0013-E006; BATCH-0054-E007). Some implementation systems formally required corrective measures, replacement, external evaluation, and follow-up, and CONEVAL reported completion of 95% of its own improvement commitments (BATCH-0051-E004; BATCH-0051-E005; BATCH-0054-E007). The record also contains positive operational learning: nuclear safety systems used drills, peer review, root-cause analysis, and corrective actions, although attribution to the president is not established (BATCH-0002-E004; BATCH-0002-E010; BATCH-0002-E012). Conversely, oversight findings were often not acted upon: CONEVAL reported that recommendations were disregarded to varying degrees, the health transition produced severe access problems, Ayotzinapa obstruction persisted despite repeated evidence and presidential orders, and the government continued defending military control after the Supreme Court invalidated it (BATCH-0052-E004; BATCH-0032-E003; BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0055-E006; BATCH-0011-E003). Personnel changes sometimes followed failure, but reassignment of implicated officials and replacement of search leadership raised doubts about corrective intent and competence (BATCH-0046-E008; BATCH-0004-E008). Adaptation was therefore observable, but not consistently evidence-led, corrective, or successful. Attribution is strongest for high-level redesign and public defense, weaker for agency-level learning and technical follow-through.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E003","BATCH-0004-E008","BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0011-E007","BATCH-0013-E006","BATCH-0054-E007","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0051-E005","BATCH-0002-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0052-E004","BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0013-E002","BATCH-0055-E006","BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0046-E008","BATCH-0004-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Formal evaluation and redesign do not prove that the ruler used findings to improve results.","The record rarely identifies a complete feedback loop from audit finding to presidential decision to verified outcome.","Some changes were reactive institutional turnover rather than demonstrated learning."]},{"question_id":"8B.9","answer":"López Obrador responded decisively to crises, opposition, and institutional resistance, often preserving his preferred political and administrative direction, but the effectiveness and legality of those responses were mixed. In security, he ordered or defended military deployment, expanded the Guard, and used the armed forces in infrastructure, migration, and public services; in the 2019 Culiacán crisis he ordered Ovidio Guzmán released to avoid further casualties (BATCH-0016-E004; BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0010-E002; BATCH-0029-E007). In electoral and judicial conflicts, he pursued Plan B and military-control reforms, criticized courts and opponents, and continued political pressure after the Supreme Court invalidated key measures (BATCH-0014-E005; BATCH-0013-E016; BATCH-0055-E006; BATCH-0012-E015). He also created an Ayotzinapa truth commission, appointed investigators, invited experts, and formally ordered military cooperation, which are favorable crisis-response elements (BATCH-0003-E016; BATCH-0013-E001). However, military agencies withheld records, the expert group withdrew, and the president defended the Army rather than compelling compliance (BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0013-E003; BATCH-0030-E012). During Hurricane Otis, the government deployed troops and began reconstruction coordination, but early distribution was delayed or uneven and the president’s public response was criticized (BATCH-0003-E022; BATCH-0031-E003; BATCH-0050-E010). Internationally, Mexico maintained diplomatic channels and proposed mediation, but evidence of influence over conflicts is limited (BATCH-0012-E014; BATCH-0045-E012). These responses show high decisional control and political resilience, but crisis management often protected regime priorities at the expense of compliance, transparency, or durable institutional control. Attribution to López Obrador is strong for policy direction and public decisions; operational outcomes remain shared with agencies, courts, military actors, criminal groups, and external shocks.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0016-E004","BATCH-0016-E002","BATCH-0010-E002","BATCH-0029-E007","BATCH-0003-E016","BATCH-0013-E001","BATCH-0003-E022","BATCH-0031-E003","BATCH-0045-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0013-E016","BATCH-0055-E006","BATCH-0013-E002","BATCH-0013-E003","BATCH-0030-E012","BATCH-0050-E010","BATCH-0012-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Some crisis outcomes are early snapshots rather than completed evaluations.","The Culiacán decision involved contested casualty and operational accounts.","The evidence cannot establish presidential control over every military, criminal, judicial, or subnational response."]},{"question_id":"8B.10","answer":"By the end of the 2023 period, López Obrador had converted substantial parts of his program into durable budgets, programs, institutions, infrastructure, and state practice, but the portfolio remained mixed, fragile, and internally contradictory. Durable advances included expanded pensions and transfers, minimum-wage gains, the National Guard and military administrative apparatus, IMSS-BIENESTAR’s federalization framework, major infrastructure assets, and continued state-led energy and development priorities (BATCH-0032-E006; BATCH-0031-E008; BATCH-0051-E001; BATCH-0029-E007; BATCH-0030-E004; BATCH-0052-E014). Poverty reduction, lower food and housing deprivation, older-person coverage, and some macroeconomic stability indicate genuine progress on selected goals (BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0032-E004; BATCH-0032-E009; BATCH-0051-E016). Yet important program components regressed or remained unresolved: health access worsened, extreme poverty increased in absolute terms, criminal impunity and violence remained high, autonomous oversight institutions were weakened, transparency deteriorated, Ayotzinapa remained unresolved, and major projects opened incomplete and over budget (BATCH-0032-E003; BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0016-E010; BATCH-0026-E020; BATCH-0013-E010; BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0030-E004). Durability is also qualified by judicial invalidation of military-control and electoral reforms, unresolved audits, dependence on military administration, and weak program indicators and logical linkages (BATCH-0055-E008; BATCH-0014-E005; BATCH-0040-E008; BATCH-0052-E006; BATCH-0054-E006). The ruler therefore achieved durable institutional and political transformation across important priorities, but not a coherent conversion of the full stated portfolio into durable outcomes. Inherited capacity, pandemic recovery, remittances, external markets, subnational implementation, subordinate resistance, and international partners complicate causal attribution. Moral approval or disapproval of the program does not affect this execution assessment.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0031-E008","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0029-E007","BATCH-0030-E004","BATCH-0052-E014","BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0032-E004","BATCH-0032-E009","BATCH-0051-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0016-E010","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0013-E010","BATCH-0013-E002","BATCH-0030-E004","BATCH-0055-E008","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0040-E008","BATCH-0052-E006","BATCH-0054-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The target period ends before several programs and projects reached mature outcomes.","Durability after the end of the presidency is only partly observable from the supplied index.","The evidence is strongest for domestic security, social transfers, health, and infrastructure, and thinner for international and nuclear objectives."]}],"cross_lens_observations":[]}
